title: 2026-12-20-quantization-technical-review-lyra-ai
summary: Redwood SE and AE walked Lyra AI through quantization tradeoffs (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ), explained KV cache and batching interactions, and reviewed preliminary benchmark results. Customer asked about accuracy regressions and how to validate across their evaluation suites. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share detailed benchmark spreadsheet and run a pilot on Lyra's internal tests; schedule follow-up to review pilot results and Dedicated capacity quote.
next_steps: Priya to share quantization benchmark spreadsheet and config used (GPTQ/AWQ/INT8) by 2026-12-22
Lyra to provide representative eval dataset and sample prompts by 2026-12-29
Redwood to run pilot on Lyra dataset (RDW-quant-pilot) and deliver delta metrics within 2 weeks of dataset receipt
Schedule follow-up deep-dive to review pilot and Dedicated capacity recommendation week of 2027-01-11
action_items: Priya Shah: export and share full quantization benchmark CSV + per-layer stats (due 2026-12-22)
Evan Park: upload sample eval set and 50 representative prompts to shared S3 (due 2026-12-29)
Alex Morgan: prepare Dedicated capacity cost estimate and pilot scope doc (due 2027-01-07)
Sofia Ruiz: provide baseline metrics (FP16) and golden outputs for 200 samples (due 2026-12-29)
transcription:
Meeting header: 2026-12-20 15:00 PST | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood Solutions), Evan (Lyra Head Infra), Sofia (Lyra ML), Tomas (Lyra CTO), Maya (Lyra SRE)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. we're going to dig into the quantization results you sent and go over tradeoffs, latency numbers, and how this will play with your VPC/on-prem plan. quick go-round for introductions.
[00:18] Evan: Evan Park, head of infra at Lyra. we're exploring moving inference back in-house for regulatory needs but want to understand the smallest quality loss we can get for big cost wins.
[00:30] Sofia: Sofia, ML engineering, i own the model eval and finetuning pipelines. we mostly run Llama-2-70B variants and some mixed-arch models.
[00:40] Tomás: Tomás, CTO. interested in production latencies for 99th, throughput for batch workloads, and the operational story for private deployments.
[00:52] Priya: Great, thanks. quick context from Redwood: we tested GPTQ and AWQ-style post-training quantization, full int8 profiles and fp8 experimental runs. our goal is to show relative latency/throughput uplift and the accuracy delta on your evals.
[01:12] Sofia: quick question — when you say AWQ, do you mean the new asymmetric weight quant method? sometimes my notes say A-W-Q and other times A-W-Q-A, sorry.
[01:21] Priya: yes AWQ as in asymmetric weight quant; sometimes our export notes call it AWQ-ptq in the spreadsheet. it's a post training method that's lighter than full GPTQ.
[01:30] Alex: i'll share the benchmark link after the call. high level takeaways first: int8 (per-tensor) gives large throughput low-latency gains but the quality regressions are model- and prompt-dependent. GPTQ gives better fidelity overall but is slower to compile and has larger memory in some variants. fp8 can be a middle ground on newer kernels.
[01:49] Evan: can you quantify 'large'? ballpark tokens/sec or percent latency reduction?
[01:55] Priya: on Redwood Dedicated on A100-style VMs: INT8 (with per-channel) improved tokens/sec by 2.2x on average for seq len 128 and reduced median token latency by ~45%. tail (p99) improved ~30% depending on batching. GPTQ typically gives 1.6x throughput but preserves perplexity within ~1-3% on our decently-sized evals. AWQ sometimes achieves 1.9x with smaller perplexity delta than naive int8. fp8 numbers we saw vary — on optimized kernels fp8 approached 1.8-2.0x.
[02:30] Sofia: those sound promising. what about accuracy regressions on generation tasks? for us, Rouge-L and factuality matter more than perplexity.
[02:37] Priya: good point. we ran generation evals — instruction-following prompts, summarization, and Q-A. GPTQ typically had the smallest Rouge-L delta (<1% on most models). AWQ had 1-3% deltas in some runs but retained most factual answers. naive int8 sometimes showed 5-10% degradation on specific heads and high-context prompts.
[02:58] Jordan: also note that per-layer breakdowns matter: embedding and early MLP layers are more sensitive; the attention projection layers sometimes tolerate more aggressive quant. our spreadsheet highlights per-layer MSE and activation histograms.
[03:15] Maya: you mentioned KV cache earlier — how does quantization interact with the KV cache and prefix caching?
[03:22] Priya: KV cache is unchanged at runtime for most of these approaches; we keep cached K/V in FP16 usually, so cold-start latency benefits are mainly from compute reduction on the forward pass. however, the memory footprint reduction from int8 helps overall working set so larger batch sizes and bigger windows are feasible before swapping. we also showed a 20-30% reduction in memory bandwidth for fused kernels.
[03:46] Evan: and batching? we're latency-sensitive but sometimes do micro-batch bursts for throughput. any guidance?
[03:51] Priya: continuous batching on Redwood is workload-aware — with int8 you can increase batch sizes and keep median latency within your SLO; but p99 can still be impacted by queueing. recommended approach: set a soft max_batch for 50ms tail and allow adaptive burst up to N for throughput jobs. we can show config that pins per-route batching and separates latency vs throughput routes.
[04:20] Sofia: operationally, what's the compile time or model preparation time for GPTQ vs AWQ vs fp8?
[04:26] Priya: GPTQ pipeline is heavier — you should expect several hours for large 70B models on a single GPU for calibration + weight updates, unless you use sharded offline tooling. AWQ and int8 PTQ are much faster, often minutes to under an hour depending on calibration samples. fp8 often requires kernel support and sometimes a short compile step but not a full pass like GPTQ.
[04:52] Tomás: if we plan on private deployment on-prem, what's the recommended stack? NA heh, runbook?
[04:58] Alex: for private we recommend Redwood Private with customer-managed control plane; for on-prem you can use our on-prem package which supports dedicated quant profiles and we can bring the optimized kernels. licensing is per-deployment; we also provide KMS integrations for model keys.
[05:15] Evan: are there any known model classes where AWQ fails badly? any gotchas?
[05:20] Priya: AWQ tends to struggle with heavily finetuned heads where weight distributions shift; we saw some failure modes with extremely peaky activation distributions — in those cases GPTQ or layerwise mixed precision is safer. also watch out for layernorm folding — some transforms introduce numeric instability under aggressive quant.
[05:40] Sofia: can Redwood's runtime do mixed precision per-layer automatically?
[05:43] Priya: yes, we support mixed-profiles. runtime can select per-layer int8/fp16 mix based on quant-stat thresholds. our profiling run suggests picking int8 for most MLPs, fp16 for embeddings and norm-adjacent layers, and fp8 where supported on kernel level.
[06:02] Jordan: another operational tip: keep a golden FP16 set and run a lightweight checker that computes BLEU/ROUGE/top-k overlap for each release. we include a regression alerting hook in Redwood Optimize.
[06:18] Evan: how do you recommend validating factuality and hallucination changes due to quant?
[06:22] Priya: use a mix of automatic checks and human eval. automated: answer similarity scoring, knowledge-augmented QA checks, and embedding-based clustering for content drift. humans for a stratified sample on high-value prompts. we can run a pilot with your FAQ and critical queries.
[06:40] Sofia: about memory — if we keep KV cache in fp16 and model weights in int8, what is the expected RAM/GPU savings?
[06:46] Priya: rough numbers: weights int8 cut model param memory to ~50-55% of fp16; with KV in fp16 the additional working memory is still significant but overall GPU footprint drops by ~35-45% depending on sequence length. that translates to either larger effective batch size or hosting larger models per GPU.
[07:10] Tomás: okay, show me an example tradeoff: if we accept a 2% Rouge-L drop, what do we get for throughput?
[07:17] Priya: from our runs on Llama-2-70B: GPTQ gives ~1.6x throughput with <1% Rouge-L drop; AWQ in tuned mode reached ~1.9x with ~1-2% drop; naive int8 hit ~2.2x but had 4-6% drop on some prompts. fp8 was around 1.8-2.0x with 1-1.5% drop but requires fp8 kernel support.
[07:45] Sofia: do you have automated tooling to re-run evals post-quant and produce per-prompt diffs?
[07:51] Jordan: yes, our eval harness emits per-prompt scoring, delta buckets, and highlights the top regressions. we can run that against your repo if you give us test vectors.
[08:03] Evan: on the compliance side — does quantization change audit log content or data handling?
[08:08] Alex: no — quantization is a model representation change; requests, tokens, and audit logs remain the same. for Private we store logs in your S3/KMS or local vault per your retention policy.
[08:20] Priya: one more note — quantized models are still subject to same model lineage rules; we tag quant profile/version so you can trace outputs to a specific quantization run.
[08:30] Sofia: any hard numbers on tail latency p99 with batching?
[08:34] Priya: sample from our bench: FP16 median token latency 12ms, p99 85ms at batch 1-2. INT8 tuned median 6.5ms, p99 60ms. With batching to 8, throughput scales ~6x but p99 can spike if queueing not bounded; recommended to use adaptive batching and per-route SLOs.
[09:02] Tomás: is there any risk of silent correctness regressions where metrics look fine but factuality drops?
[09:08] Priya: yes, that's possible. automatic metrics like BLEU/ROUGE won't always capture hallucination. that's why sampling and targeted factual QA checks are critical; we recommend a two-stage gating: automated diffs plus manual review on a stratified sample of the high-value prompt set.
[09:26] Sofia: for our pilot, we want to test Llama-2-70B instruction tuned with our in-house finetune. if we give you the weights can Redwood run GPTQ internally or do we need to do offline?
[09:35] Priya: we can run GPTQ in both modes. for Private or on-prem you can run our offline toolchain. for a hosted pilot on Dedicated we can run it in your reserved pool with encrypted storage. either way we recommend a cal sample set of 1k-5k tokens for calibration.
[09:55] Evan: license question — any IP risks from GPTQ runs?
[09:58] Alex: GPTQ is a transformation on weights; legal depends on your model license. operationally we don't expose weights outside your VPC when on Private/on-prem; for Hosted/Dedicated we use encrypted storage controlled by you for the pilot. we'd loop legal if you want written guidance.
[10:15] Jordan: quick note on model variants: you can keep FP16 golden for critical routes and use quantized variants as cheaper fallbacks. runtime supports automatic fallback if quality drops below a threshold.
[10:28] Sofia: that fallback — is it route-level or token-level?
[10:32] Priya: currently route-level and call-level; token-level switching is researchy and expensive. we do automatic A/B canaries and rollback on regression alerts.
[10:41] Tomás: operational concerns — how do you handle model rollbacks and versioning for quant profiles?
[10:46] Alex: we version quant profiles with a UUID and store provenance in the model registry. rollbacks are atomic in the control plane; you can route a percentage back to FP16 or previous quant profile during a canary.
[11:00] Evan: what about on-prem hardware — are there particular GPU families we should target for fp8 kernels?
[11:05] Priya: latest Ampere+ and H100 families have fp8 and faster tensor core support; some fp8 kernels are vendor-optimized for Hopper. for older GPUs, int8 with optimized kernels is the safer cross-hardware choice. we'll share a compatibility matrix.
[11:23] Sofia: curious — how often do you see model-specific oddities where a single layer causes big drop?
[11:28] Priya: fairly often for heavily finetuned heads or quantization-unfriendly vocabs. our per-layer analysis usually reveals a handful of sensitive layers; we then apply mixed precision or bias-correction. GPTQ tends to handle those better since it adjusts weight updates per layer.
[11:45] Jordan: action item reminder — we'll provide the per-layer MSE visualizations in the spreadsheet.
[11:50] Alex: ok wrapping up, recap: share spreadsheet & config (Priya), Lyra uploads eval set (Evan), Redwood runs pilot and returns per-prompt diffs, and Alex to send Dedicated quote.
[12:03] Tomás: good — last question: SLA implications for quantized models on Dedicated?
[12:08] Alex: quantized models don't change SLA commitments; latency targets are measured on live traffic and we have per-route SLOs. if quantization reduces variability we can often tighten tails; we'll partner on SLO setting during onboarding.
[12:21] Sofia: thanks, appreciate the thoroughness.
[12:24] Alex: thanks everyone. i'll send the link and next steps.

End of transcript.
